signals.title: Meet Relate by Neo4j: An Embedded Database for AI Agents
signals.excerpt:
Today, at NODES 2026, we’re launching Relate by Neo4j: an open-source, embedded graph database that keeps the connections along with the facts. It helps your agents build and understand relationships in any data, running inside whatever your agent is already using: as a library in your application, a CLI tool in your sandbox, or a WebAssembly build in your browser. A single command installs it, and there’s no server to deploy. Relate starts and stops with your application, with nothing to keep running.

## Built for Agents

Agents increasingly choose their own tools, and they choose the ones that are easiest to start with. So we designed Relate for the agent first. A single line installs Relate and adds its skill to a coding agent, and from then on the agent can turn data into a connected graph for queries on its own. For agents you build, add Relate as a library in Python, Javascript, Rust, Java, Go, or Swift, and the database ships with your agent, with no server to deploy. Agents that never open a shell can connect over MCP: relate serve turns a database into tools for reading schema and running queries.

...

Relate is a new Rust implementation, built on twenty years of Neo4j graph experience. It is an open-source, lightweight library you embed in your agents, with millisecond startup and submillisecond queries for ephemeral sessions and durable storage for persistent ones. Four things set it apart:

- Full Cypher and GQL coverage – Relate runs more than 30k test scenarios for openCypher, Cypher 25 and GQL to assert that it is compatible with the Neo4j query surface
- Fast and smart graph query engine with many of the approaches that are used in modern databases and also in Neo4j’s query engine.
- Relationships and similarity fit within one query. A single Cypher statement can follow connections and run vector and full-text search together, so your agent doesn’t stitch results from two stores together in glue code.
- We’ve built Relate to be agent-native from the first command. The skill and MCP endpoint ship with Relate, and agent mode returns output the agent can process optimally. Your agent can install it and start querying without any wiring from you.

...

Relate is open source and available today, and your agent can set it up itself. Paste this into your coding agent:

```
Install Relate by Neo4j by following the instructions at relatedb.ai. 
Use Relate as this project's memory: 
store what you learn as connected facts, and query them with Cypher.Code language: PHP (php)

```

# Releasing MACaQ: one quantizer across modalities

Introducing MACaQ for text, images, audio, video and 3D, with an Apache 2.0 implementation, a paper and an interactive guide.

We are releasing MACaQ, short for Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization: one quantization recipe for low-precision weights and activations, with examples spanning text, images, audio, video and 3D reconstruction.

The MACaQ implementation is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

## One common building block

Different model architectures share a building block: the linear layer. MACaQ keeps balancing, rotation and quantization decisions local to that layer, avoiding architecture-specific changes to neighboring layers. Calibration and refinement prepare the weights offline; lightweight input transforms are applied during inference.

...

The MACaQ interactive blog brings the method to life through visual and audio comparisons, an explanation of the layer-local design, measured model-size and quality comparisons, and integration workflows for llama.cpp and vLLM. Image and video workflows also use Diffusers.

signals.title: Compile the Knowledge at Index Time
signals.excerpt:
That repeated work is what RAGFlow 1.0 is built to remove. InfiniFlow now positions the open-source engine as a supply layer for retrieval agents rather than an end-to-end RAG pipeline, and the mechanism behind the repositioning is knowledge compilation: move the understanding from query time to index time. Compile once, when a document arrives, and store the result as artifacts the agent can use directly, instead of re-deriving the same understanding inside every prompt.

Compilation produces several artifact types from the same documents. There is a navigation tree over chapters and sections. There is an entity graph, timelines for collections that change over time, and wikis an enterprise can choose to generate. And there are atomic propositions, the piece the rest of this post is about.

A proposition is a one-sentence fact extracted from the source, paired with a verbatim quote. The quote has to be a contiguous substring of the original text, and that is checked mechanically. A proposition whose quote does not match the source word for word does not count as evidence.

...

What moved the numbers was attaching claim-evidence pairs to the tree's leaves. When the evidence at a leaf is sufficient to answer, the agent answers from the evidence and skips reading the raw chunk entirely. The paper reports that this cuts query tokens by 91% when the evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not — a 38% average reduction, at a measured sufficiency rate near 43% against a break-even of about 2%.

Read those as the team's numbers, from the team's runs: a harness built on BM25 and grep-style search with a single model, MiniMax M3, measured on BrowseComp-Plus and FRAMES. They are not independent benchmarks, and nobody should plan capacity around the decimals. The shape matters more than the figures. A compiled hit is cheap to use. A miss costs almost nothing, because the system checks the evidence before the model starts searching and, if the set is not enough, discards the whole block and searches as it would have anyway. ... It has to win occasionally and lose cheaply.

signals.title: Building Graph-Enhanced GenAI Applications with graphrag-toolkit - KDnuggets
signals.excerpt:
Learn how graph-enhanced RAG connects related facts that plain vector search misses, then build a multi-hop research assistant with AWS Labs' open-source graphrag-toolkit, Neo4j, and pgvector. 

By Shittu Olumide, Technical Content Specialist on November 12, 2026 in Language Models

...

Graph-enhanced RAG, usually shortened to GraphRAG, is retrieval that queries a knowledge graph rather than a plain vector index, so an application can follow actual relationships between pieces of information instead of only finding text that sounds similar to the question. Neo4j's own explainer frames this as combining the retrieval strengths of a knowledge graph — explicit entities and the relationships between them — with the generative fluency of a large language model (LLM), so the model reasons over connected facts rather than isolated fragments of text.

...

## Introducing graphrag-toolkit

The graphrag-toolkit is an open-source, Apache 2.0-licensed Python toolkit built by AWS Labs specifically to close that gap. It's made up of two components. The first, and the focus of this article, is lexical-graph, a framework for automatically building a hierarchical knowledge graph from unstructured documents and querying it. The second, BYOKG-RAG (Bring Your Own Knowledge Graph), is a separate approach for teams that already have a knowledge graph and want a multi-strategy question-answering layer over it, without re-extracting anything from scratch.

...

This is the technical core worth understanding before writing any code. Per the toolkit's own graph model documentation, a lexical graph organizes extracted content into six connected levels: source, chunk, topic, statement, fact, and entity. Retrieval can hop between any of these levels rather than being stuck retrieving only at the chunk level the way a plain vector store is, which is the structural feature that makes multi-hop questions actually answerable.

...

## Querying: Traversal-Based Search

Here's the actual query mechanism, sourced directly from the toolkit's querying documentation. A user's question first gets embedded, and that embedding runs a top-K similarity search against the vector store to find anchor points: statements or chunks that look relevant on the surface. Those anchors then seed one or more graph traversal queries, which pull in thematically connected content from across the graph, not just the chunks that scored highest on similarity alone. The retrieved content, grouped by topic and source, is then supplied to an LLM alongside the original question to generate the actual answer.

One genuinely current fact is easy to miss: the toolkit also ships an older semantic-guided search strategy, but the documentation states directly that it's likely to be retired in a future release. Traversal-based search is both the current default and the one worth building against today, which is exactly the approach used in the hands-on build below.

...

| Layer | Built-in options |
| --- | --- |
| Graph store | Amazon Neptune Database, Amazon Neptune Analytics, Neo4j, FalkorDB |
| Vector store | Amazon Neptune (DB and Analytics), Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Postgres (with pgvector), Amazon S3 Vectors |
| Foundation model provider | Amazon Bedrock (the only built-in option; extensible to other providers with custom work) |

Neo4j and Postgres with pgvector are the two options that can run entirely locally in Docker at zero infrastructure cost, which is exactly why this tutorial builds around that combination. One small caveat on FalkorDB specifically: the toolkit's repository keeps FalkorDB support in a separate `lexical-graph-contrib/falkordb` package rather than bundling it into the core `graphrag-lexical-graph` install, so you need that additional package if you go that route instead of Neo4j. The one piece that can't currently be swapped out without extra engineering effort is the model provider: Amazon Bedrock is what the toolkit is configured to use by default, so an AWS account with Bedrock model access enabled is unavoidable for this build, even though the graph

...

pip install graphrag-lexical-graph
pip install psycopg2-binary pgvector
pip install llama-index-readers-web html2text

...

`graphrag-lexical-graph` is the actual PyPI package name for the lexical-graph library, confirmed directly on its PyPI page; it is currently in the 3.18.x release series and requires Python 3.10 or greater. The Postgres vector store specifically requires both `psycopg2-binary` and `pgvector` as separate dependencies, per the toolkit's own Postgres vector store documentation. `llama-index-readers-web` supplies `SimpleWebPageReader`, used to pull in the source articles below, and `html2text` is its own required dependency specifically when `html_to_text=True` is passed, per the reader's own source.

...

The lexical-graph can expose a tenant's graph as a callable tool through a Model Context Protocol server, letting an agent browse a catalog of domain-specific graphs and pick the right one for a given question automatically. Multi-tenancy lets you host several separate graphs — different document collections, different users — inside the same underlying graph and vector stores rather than provisioning new infrastructure per tenant. Metadata filtering lets you constrain both indexing and querying to specific document subsets based on tags you attach yourself. And versioned updates handle the real-world case this tutorial's one-shot build ignored entirely: re-ingesting a document that's since changed, archiving the old version automatically rather than leaving stale, contradictory information in the graph.

signals.title: An Agent That Searches, Outlines, and Reads Entire Documents Outperforms Chunk-and-Embed Retrieval
signals.excerpt:
# Retrieval for RAG-Resistant Docs An agent that searches, outlines, and reads entire documents outperforms chunk-and-embed retrieval

Published Nov 13, 2026

Retrieving documents chunk by chunk works well with many types of text, but it can fail with documents in which the meaning of a given span — say, numbers in a table — depends on particulars found elsewhere on the page — say, the label of their units. Researchers assigned agents to keep all the necessary information in view. 

What’s new: Sagar Tamang, Ayush Vyas, and Tabarakul Hazarika at Indian Institute of Technology Patna and TwoSpoon, an independent tech lab, developed Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search (READ). Their method replaces vector-based retrieval with an agentic harness and specialized search tools. 

Key insight: For RAG-style retrieval, a document is divided into chunks that are embedded, and a model retrieves chunks whose embeddings are similar to the embedding of the query. But this approach can fail with documents such as financial or scientific reports, where numbers in a table gain important meaning from units or dates that may lie many lines away, or legal briefs, in which words may have special meanings that are defined many paragraphs away. An agent with tools to navigate undivided documents can look beyond predefined chunks.

How it works: The authors used the READ method with Gemini 2.5 Pro.

- The system had access to three tools: (i) A keyword-search tool returned matching line numbers, (ii) an outline tool listed section headings with line numbers, and (iii) a text-reader tool fetched specific line ranges.
- Given a query like, “What is the mathematical difference between the Fiscal Deficit and the Revenue Surplus for the year 2024-2025?,” the READ agent activated a loop that generated a search term such as “Fiscal Deficit,” scanned a document for the term, checked matching line(s) against the document outline, and read the text from the table headers to the matching line(s).
- Within the loop, the model refined its query when it got too many hits, too few hits, or insufficient information to make sense of what it found. Each refinement repeated the loop with a new search term or a new range to be read.

Results: The authors used READ, RAG-style retrieval, and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop to answer 51 questions about a 780-page financial report published by the government of Gujarat, India. All systems were based on Gemini 2.5 Pro. READ answered 58.8 percent of the questions correctly, outperforming both RAG-style retrieval (15.7 percent) and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop (27.5 percent)

signals.title: AMD Quark quantizes Qwen3.8-Flash-Next to UINT4 for 128 GB Ryzen AI Halo edge deployment
signals.excerpt:
AMD's Quark quantization toolkit enables Qwen3.8-Flash-Next to run on Ryzen AI Halo's unified memory by compressing expert weights to UINT4 and replacing the 51 GB FP8 n-gram table with a 1.3 GB calibrated per-token lookup, cutting checkpoint storage from ~130 GB to ~80 GB.

...

AMD has published a technical evaluation demonstrating how its Quark quantization framework can fit the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next large language model onto consumer-grade Ryzen AI Halo hardware with 128 GB of unified memory. The approach combines activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) to compress routed expert weights to 4-bit unsigned integers (UINT4) with a novel replacement for the model's massive n-gram lookup table. Rather than loading the ~51 GB FP8 n-gram table, AMD tested a calibrated per-token table of only ~1.3 GB that supplies token-specific vectors without local context dependency, plus a zero-lookup baseline for comparison.

The evaluation measures accuracy tradeoffs across thinking and non-thinking modes on benchmarks including MMLU-Pro, coding tasks, and parallel tool-calling. Results show that several thinking-mode scores remain stable even without the full n-gram table, while the calibrated per-token table recovers most of the accuracy loss from zero lookup on non-thinking benchmarks. This work addresses a concrete deployment constraint: unified memory architectures like Ryzen AI Halo cannot offload the n-gram table to separate CPU memory without consuming the same shared pool, making table compression essential for leaving room for the KV cache and runtime buffers.

...

- UINT4 AWQ expert quantization: AMD Quark applies activation-aware weight quantization with group size 128 to the model's routed expert weights, reducing precision from BF16 to 4-bit unsigned integers as the foundation for edge deployment.
- N-gram table architecture: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next uses bigram and trigram hashing at Layer 2 to retrieve learned vectors from a context-dependent table, distinct from ordinary token embeddings; this table contributes ~102 GB in BF16 or ~51 GB in FP8 to checkpoint storage.
- Calibrated per-token replacement (U): A ~1.3 GB table providing one fixed vector per token ID, independent of preceding context, replaces the full n-gram lookup; ordinary token embeddings, output head, and downstream layers remain unmodified.
- Memory-constrained deployment target: Ryzen AI Halo's unified memory architecture means CPU/GPU memory is not separable; the ~130 GB FP8-table checkpoint leaves insufficient headroom for OS, KV cache, and runtime buffers on 128 GB systems.
- Accuracy evaluation scope: Tests cover xhigh reasoning-effort thinking mode, MMLU-Pro, coding benchmarks, and parallel tool-calling with response-length analysis; the calibrated U table recovers most non-thinking accuracy loss versus zero lookup while maintaining several thinking-mode scores.

Developed as the first research initiative under Scale's collaboration with IMDA, the benchmark evaluates 19 AI models across 1,860 legal scenarios spanning 10 domains of Singaporean law.

...

SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 original questions written by qualified legal professionals with expertise in Singapore law. The questions cover 10 legal domains, including criminal law, employment, property, family law, and judicial processes.

signals.excerpt:
# I made my AI agent's notes vault retrievable: 35 MB embedder, llama.cpp reranker, corrections as regression tests 

Ok, I made a thing! LLMs have their... quirks. Namely re-reading the same notes, wandering back and forth, and spending 10x more tokens than needed because I can't be explicit.

So I built Haystack — a semantic router for a markdown vault. Instead of the agent digging through files, it queries: hybrid retrieval (embeddings + corpus-IDF term stats, RRF-fused, cross-encoder reranking via llama.cpp), all local, zero cloud, one 35 MB model, ~10 ms per query. MIT, one-command setup: github.com/diogocccarvalho/haystack.

...

Your corrections become regression tests. Every retrieval miss you fix becomes a permanent rule AND a QA pair. The audit reindexes and runs every pair — it exits 1 on a regression, so the same question can't silently fail twice.

And the learned rules only pin when they actually beat retrieval: a stored phrasing must outrank the corpus' own best hit for the same query. Scale-free, not absolute-threshold — so swapping embedders doesn't break your corrections. I A/B'd models against frozen QA sets and rejected two (a reranker that was 2x faster but -16pp Recall@3; a 97M embedder at -7pp). Numbers in docs/RESEARCH.md.

...

## Try it 

```
./setup.sh --start          # model + config + embeddings server, one command
python3 haystack.py reindex
python3 haystack.py query "that thing about the invoices"

```

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works instead (Ollama, LM Studio, remote API). Python 3.11+, stdlib + numpy only — no framework, no vector DB daemon, no cloud.

Nov 12, 2026 Research

# Introducing OWE-Bench for Long-Horizon Engineering Projects

Jacob Cole, Cindy Yang, Aravind Selvan, Daniel Babalola, and Bertie Vidgen

Jacob Cole, Cindy Yang, Aravind Selvan, Daniel Babalola, and Bertie Vidgen

Today we're releasing OpenWorldEngineer (OWE-Bench), a frontier coding benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering and research tasks across software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing.

We built OWE-Bench to test whether AI agents can make real progress on long-horizon engineering projects, ranging from GPU kernels to aircraft design. Every task is graded on unseen cases and scored on a continuous scale. This means that an agent that speeds up a program halfway to the ceiling earns 50% rather than a pass-or-fail zero.

Claude Fable 5.2 tops the current leaderboard with a score of 54.6%, using an average of 211 million tokens per task attempt. GPT-6 Astra follows with a score of 44.2% using 89 million tokens, and Claude Opus 5.5 at 41.6% using 253 million tokens. No model is close to the benchmark ceiling. Fable 5.2 leads all four domains, with Astra within a few points in physical engineering and scientific computing. The benchmark also successfully differentiates between small and large models, with Inkling and Beam only scoring 1.1% and 3.3% respectively.

...

Tasks for OWE-Bench come in two shapes. In scaffolded tasks, the agent starts from a working codebase and pushes a measurable target such as kernel speed, latency, or error. In end-to-end tasks, it builds the whole artifact from a bare environment: a trained model, a data pipeline, a mechanical design. Depending on the task, agents get 4 to 18 hours per attempt (median 8), for 257 agent-hours across one pass over all tasks, on hardware matched to the task, such as a CPU sandbox, NVIDIA H100 or B300. Seven tasks use a GPU.

 

The 26 tasks span four domains:

- Software engineering (8 tasks): databases, data pipelines, interpreters, and layout, such as exactly-once streaming payments ETL into Iceberg tables with alerts under fault injection
- Physical engineering (5 tasks): CAD reconstruction, structural design, and aircraft, such as a parametric Design/Build/Fly electric aircraft scored over 34 hidden flights spanning three missions
- Machine learning (7 tasks): GPU kernels, training, and inference, such as post-training Qwen3-8B on chess tactics through a metered training service, scored on 1,000 private puzzles
- Scientific computing (6 tasks): chemistry and earth-science modeling, such as relocating an earthquake sequence from supplied seismic observations

...

Evaluation begins with agents submitting an artifact, like a model checkpoint, a data pipeline, a kernel package, a CAD program, or an aircraft design. They are then scored offline by an independent verifier operating without network access, testing the deliverable on CPUs and GPUs using ... Performance is measured strictly through execution, simulation, or geometric analysis rather than model judgments.

...

Fable 5.2 leads in every domain. It scores 62.2% in software engineering against 49.7% for Claude Opus 5.5 (+12.2pp), and 54.6% in machine learning against 47.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (+6.8pp). The gap with the next best model is far smaller in physical engineering (59.6% vs. 57.3%) and scientific computing (40.2% vs. 39.4%), where GPT-6 Astra is within the margin of error.

signals.title: End‑to‑End 4‑Bit Training - Thinking Machines Lab
signals.excerpt:
# End‑to‑End 4‑Bit Training

Jack Cook in collaboration with others at Thinking Machines Nov 13, 2026

...

Training large language models involves calculating and storing a lot of numbers. Using fewer bits for each value reduces memory usage and allows GPUs to perform calculations faster. However, there is a tradeoff: fewer bits also mean fewer representable numbers, leading to more aggressive rounding. Lower-precision representations ultimately hurt accuracy by adding error to the calculations.

...

We manage this tradeoff through our use of three key numerical formats during training: BF16, MXFP8, and NVFP4. Each format’s precision is fixed, but its speed depends on the hardware being used. We train on NVIDIA’s Grace Blackwell Ultra platform, the GB300, which is designed to optimize matrix multiplications with NVFP4. Notably, NVFP4 is stored with 3.6x fewer bits than BF16, but it runs up to 6x faster on GB300s.

...

In training Inkling 2 Small, we made the following decisions:

- NVFP4 precision in the expert layers for forward passes, bolstered by a dedicated kernel.
- MXFP8 precision for backward passes with re-quantization and stochastic rounding, techniques for reducing gradient bias.
- Quantization techniques for accelerating GPU communications, which alleviated a bottleneck that surfaced after we sped up computation.

Inkling 2 Small is the largest model we are aware of that was trained end-to-end with a native 4-bit forward pass. We configure numerics in the same way from the start of pretraining through the final RL rollout. This makes training simpler and eliminates the need for calibration when a quantized checkpoint is delivered at the end of training. In our largest jobs, this recipe provides us with an 8% wall-clock speedup in pretraining and a 20% speedup in RL over full MXFP8 training. In this post, we explain the details that made this possible.

...

With our new NVFP4 matrix multiplications (GEMMs), our MoE layer’s forward pass should theoretically have gotten about three times faster compared to our MXFP8 implementation. But after reducing precision, we noticed we were running up against a bottleneck: communications during expert parallelism.

Since MoE layers are often very large, it is common to split up experts between different GPUs. When computing the MoE layer, a small router decides where each token should go, and tokens are then dispatched to the GPUs containing the routed experts. After completing the GEMMs, the computations of these routed experts are returned to the source GPU and combined to create the MoE layer’s final output. On an NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system, the tokens will typically be sent over NVLink, which has a bandwidth of 900 GB/s in each direction. At the same time, the NVFP4 GEMMs will run at a speed of up to 15 PFLOPS. Dividing one by the other, each GPU could perform as many as 16,000 floating point operations in the time it takes to receive a single byte. Unless every byte that arrives brings at least that much computation with it, the Tensor Cores sit idle waiting on NVLink.

We found this imbalance created bottlenecks where either the MoE GEMMs were unable to execute because they were waiting to receive the dispatched tokens, or the following operation (in Inkling 2 Small, short convolutions) was unable to start because it was waiting to receive the combined tokens. During dispatch, we avoid this issue by dispatching tokens in NVFP4. Like Quartet II, our backward pass is computed using quantized — not high-precision — activations from the forward pass (note the input to the weight gradient, or WGRAD, computation in Figure 4), which reduces the amount of data sent over NVLink enough to alleviate the dispatch bottleneck. During combine, however, the output activations need to remain in higher precision (by default, BF16) to avoid impairing model performance.

We alleviate the communications bottleneck by quantizing the data transmitted during combine as well. We initially experimented with quantizing the resulting activations to MXFP8, but found that this impaired performance too much due to MXFP8’s poor representation of outlier values. Instead, we found that performing a 32-dimensional random Hadamard transform (RHT) and then quantizing to block-scaled S2F6, another 8-bit format, resulted in no measurable accuracy degradation during training.

signals.title: NVIDIA Runs 753-Billion-Parameter GLM-5.3 Across Two DGX Stations | TokenPost
signals.excerpt:
An NVIDIA demonstration ran the 753-billion-parameter GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model across two connected DGX Stations, showing how local inference can serve a model whose weights exceed one GB300 GPU’s memory.

The model needs about 464 GB of GPU memory for its weights, compared with 252 GB of HBM3e memory on a single GB300 GPU. GLM-5.3 has 753 billion parameters in total and activates 40 billion for each token it generates. The model uses a mixture-of-experts design, so the full set of weights must remain available as tokens are routed to different experts.

NVIDIA linked two GB300 GPUs using ConnectX-8 RDMA and split the model’s tensors and computation between them with tensor parallelism. Station A runs an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, while Station B works as a worker. Both systems process each request, and Station A returns the completed response.

The deployment used vLLM with prefix caching, an FP8 key-value (KV) cache and multi-token prediction. On the SPEED-Bench Coding dataset, throughput reached 607.8 tokens per second with 16 requests running at once. At 32 concurrent requests, the system delivered 385 tokens per second, and mean request latency was 453.5 seconds. Concurrency refers to the number of requests being handled at the same time.

The setup called for two DGX Stations running Linux and a network connection validated with NVIDIA’s Connect Two DGX Stations playbook. Requirements also included Docker, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and access to the dataset and licenses. Each station also required 464 GB of available storage for the model checkpoint, plus space for the vLLM container and temporary files.

signals.title: MACaQ quantizes 122B model to W4A4 in 64 min on 32.5GB GPU | AI Weekly
signals.excerpt:
# MACaQ quantizes 122B model to W4A4 in 64 min on 32.5GB GPU 

 By Alexis Dufresne · Published November 12, 2026 at 03:56 UTC · Updated November 12, 2026 at 04:00 UTC 

## TL;DR

- MACaQ quantizes a 122-billion-parameter model to MXFP4 W4A4 in 64 minutes using only 32.5GB of GPU RAM.
- On Llama-3-8B it matches DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ perplexity in 11 times less quantization time, adding 2.3% overhead on Qwen3-32B in vLLM.
- Treating every linear layer independently removes cross-layer basis-transform propagation and lets calibration stream one layer at a time.

Quantizing a 122B model to W4A4 in an hour on 32.5GB of GPU RAM collapses the engineering and hardware cost of frontier-scale low-precision inference; the lever for margin-sensitive inference teams is now simpler, cheaper calibration, not marginally better compression.

MACaQ, a new post-training quantization method, compresses a 122-billion-parameter model to MXFP4 W4A4 in 64 minutes using 32.5GB of GPU RAM, according to a paper on arXiv by Lorenz K. Muller, Philippe Bich, Chiara Boretti, Hyun-Min Chang, Jiawei Zhuang and Lukas Cavigelli. The authors report matching the perplexity of DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ on Llama-3-8B in "11 times less quantization time," while adding only "2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM."

The speed comes from treating every linear layer independently, avoiding the cross-layer propagation of basis transforms that prior W4A4 methods required. "Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time," the paper states.

The method pairs a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform on activations with a new "Flip-Refinement" procedure, described as a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. The authors also apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, which they offer as evidence that the layer-local design generalizes beyond language models.

The abstract publishes no downstream task accuracy numbers and does not identify which 122B model was used for the headline 64-minute result.
